translation:
The saints split [the divine name] into its "ra" sound and its "m" sound, and gave the opinion that the "m" sound is in the form of maya (illusion), while the "ra" sound is the complete Brahman. Therefore the saints have embraced the "ra" sound. In the Kuvarpura Samagam it is written thus:

_Kabir nav lakh tara ugia, suraj koti hazar_
_Take timir bhange nahi, gor bina ghor andhar ||1||_
(Meaning: Even if nine hundred thousand stars were to rise, and thousands of millions of suns were to rise — that much light in the darkness of maya — still, for one who has not found a true Guru, the dense darkness of maya remains for him.)

Revered Yadunath Maharaj, in Note No. 50, "Pravas Sahayak" 6, page 166, has written a verse of salutation to every Guru in the Guru lineage, from Narayan down to the present day.

_Lakshminath samarambha nathyamun madhyamam_
_Asmadacharya paryantam vande guru paramparam ||1||_
(Meaning: Beginning with Narayan, the husband of Lakshmi, and including those who came in between such as Nath Muni and Yamunacharya, down to our own teachers to this day — I bow to every single Guru of this Guru lineage.)

This calculus of division and multiplication is understood only by one who has received the grace of Namdev and Kabir; only such a person can grasp this matter. Such compassion had indeed fallen upon Jivanji Maharaj, and so the true path was revealed to him. His worldly deeds and qualities had already been exhausted, and now, in surrender to the true Guru alone, he had only to recognize the Supreme Brahman. Further, through the meeting (samagam) that took place with the Guru, Jivanji Maharaj's inner eye opened, and he recognized the illusion (maya) of the world. That which he had had to wait for now stood before him of its own accord; what is difficult to attain had now become effortless. There was no need to wait any longer — Truth itself was now ready to come and sit before him. So on that day, that is, on the thirteenth of the bright half of Aso, Jivanji Maharaj went to meet Gopaldas and spent twenty-four hours in his company (samagam); through what unfolded there, the path of Truth was revealed to him. Therefore, two days later, that is, on the fifteenth of the bright half of Aso, Jivanji Maharaj, saying "Ramkabir," bowed to Gopaldas and confirmed him as his true Guru. Thus, on this day, the two of them were bound in the relationship of Guru and disciple. Jivanji Maharaj himself gives testimony to this.

_Sadguru das Gopalji, je Janakvansh avatar_
_Raghupati batayo Jivana, je Vrishabhan suta shanagar ||1||_
_Naam hamaro Jivana, kanabi kul avatar_
_Sai hamara Ramji, sadguru das Gopal ||2||_
_Kabir Ramkrishnathe ko bada, un guru seva kin_
_O to jagatke ishta the, pan guru aage aadhin ||3||_
(Meaning: Jivanji Maharaj says: My true Guru is the Vaishnav Gopaldas, who is of the Janak lineage. He has given me the vision of Raghupati [Ram], the beloved lord (Krishna) adorning Vrishabhan's daughter (Radhaji). My own name is Jivandas; I was born into the Kanbi [farming] caste. My chosen deity is Ramji, and my true Guru is the Vaishnav Gopaldasji. Addressing his Guru Gopaldasji, Jivanji Maharaj recites a couplet of Kabirji: that Ram and Krishna, though forms of the Supreme Brahman incarnate, still had to go to a Guru. Thus, whoever is born into this world, however great a ruler he may be, must still bow before a Guru. Ram and Krishna, though the chosen deities of the world, are themselves subordinate before the Guru. In this way, every person must take a Guru.)

Here, Jivanji Maharaj, having confirmed Gopaldasji as his Guru, gives the entire Guru lineage. Introducing the first Guru, he says that Gopaldasji is of the Janak lineage, and his original seat is Choranda. 1) His Guru is Dada Sukhji, who is known as being of the Pipa lineage and is a native of Shuklatirth. 2) His Guru is Gnaniji Maharaj. 3) Dwarkadasji 4) Narharidasji 5) Sari Ramdasji 6) Krishnadas Payahari 7) Karmachandji 8) Gemji 9) Joganandji 10) Anantanandji 11) Ramanandji 12) Radhavanandji 13) Hariananda 14) Devacharaj 15) Ramanidh 16) Ramanuj 17) Saraswati Bhatt 18) Lala Charaj 19) Acharya Jayamat 20) Ramanij 21) Kul Tarak 22) Ramayansh 23) Jayamatmuni 24) Ramamisar 25) Pundarik 26) Nathmuni 27) Mangalmuni 28) Bopadev Bhagavatlu 29) Shathgop 30) Sudhin 31) Muni Praj 32) Vishvaksen 33) Lakshmiji 34) Narayan.

Dada Sukhji:

In the Barot community, people are identified by lineages such as Janakvanshi, Pipavanshi, Hanumanvansh, and so on. Thus Gopaldasji was of the Janak lineage, and his Guru Dada Sukhji was of the Pipa lineage. In the Bhaktamal, a devotee named Lakhaji is called Vanaravanshi (of the monkey lineage). Of Nabha Swami too it is said that he was of the Dom lineage. People of castes such as Dom, Kalavant, Dhadhi, Bhaar, Kathak, and so on are of a kind that make their living through the art of singing.

Dr. Kantikumar Bhatt has called Gopaldas a Vanik (merchant), but this is a mistake — Gopaldasji was a Barot. Mr. Bhatt has written that because Gopaldas was as detached from the world as King Janak, he was therefore called Janakvanshi. But "Janakvanshi" and similar terms are actually sub-caste surnames used to identify one's own sub-division within the community. Gopaldasji's Guru, Dada Sukhji, was likewise of the Pipa lineage — so he too was not a Brahmin but a Barot. However, Mr. Bhatt has mistakenly described him as a Brahmin of Shinor.

Writing about Shukdev (Sukhji), Mr. Bhatt says that it is learned from the seat (gadi) of Gnaniji that he was a Brahmin of Shinor, and that he had paralysis in his left leg; he was brought to Gnaniji at Mota Sanja, and through Gnaniji's medicine the ailment was cured, after which he became Gnaniji's disciple. He had land and a house in Shinor, and lived by the priestly (yajaman) profession. It was Gnaniji who gave the Guru-mantra, the Name of Ram-Kabir. He used to recite the Bhagavat Katha at the Vyas temple near Karnali; the Maharajas of Vadodara had built a temple and rest-houses (dharmashalas) there. In one of his own couplets, Gnaniji mentions Shukdev's devotion to his Guru — that whoever serves the Guru truly, in thought, word, and deed, is saved; and to see the proof of this, he says, Shukdev is the witness:

_Manasa vacha karmana, jin kini gurusev_
_Gyani sohi ubra, sakshi suno Shukdev ||3||_
(Meaning: Those who have served their Guru with mind, speech, and action have been saved — hear that the witness to this is Shukdev.)

Shukdev could also be Vyas's son, but Mr. Bhatt has stated that this couplet refers to Sukhji. Whichever the case, Sukhji was Gnaniji's disciple, and he was not a Brahmin but a Barot; and people of the Barot community make their living through the priestly (yajaman) profession alone. Jivanji Maharaj's Guru, Gopaldas, was likewise a Barot — and moreover, in the ledger (chopdo) of the Barot who recorded Jivanji Maharaj's genealogy, a record of the generations from Jivanji Maharaj down to the present day has been entered. In their ledger, on page 412, it is written:

"Shri Jivanji Maharaj, of the Leva Patidar Amin family of village Karamsad, renounced his own house, mansion, and estate, and took up the path of teaching. He was born in his home village of Karamsad, Samvat 1649.

Shri Jivanji Maharaj manifested at the age of 11, in Samvat 1660, on Shravan Sud 8, in village Goriyad. At village Keslu, at the age of 16, spiritual discourse (gnan-goshti) took place with Mahant Gopaldasji of Choranda; village Choranda, Samvat 1683.

At village Choranda, Mahant Gopaldasji had the name of his disciple Jivanji Maharaj recorded; a gold armlet of one and a quarter tola, and 125 rupees and a shawl were given. After staying four years in village Choranda, he set out on pilgrimage to the Four Dhams, Samvat 1687, Ashadh Sud 10. He held a feast (bhandaro); a mare and 51 rupees and a pitambar (silk garment) were given. In village Mangleswar he performed six months of austerity (bhajan-bhakti). In Samvat 1717, Magsar Sud 2, the second day, he redeemed Bhoja Gujar. He held a feast; 51 rupees were placed on a copper vessel, and a silk abotiyu (upper cloth) was given. He stayed at village Mangleshwar, Samvat 1716, Jeth Sudi 2; village Dhanor, Samvat 1726, Bhadarva Sud 11.

Second [record] — At village Choranda, Dada Sukhji held a feast and a Bhagavat parayan (recitation); 125 rupees, a vessel of banat (broadcloth), and a gold ring were given, Samvat 1650. Under Dada Sukhji, the name of Gopaldasji was recorded; he was born into the Janak lineage, Samvat 1555.

Near village Kandari, in Puniyad country, Gujarat, Jivanji Maharaj held a feast, Samvat 1726; gold bangles, a dushala (shawl), and 125 rupees were given.

At Puniyad, Jivanji Maharaj built a new temple, Samvat 1730; he held a consecration festival, fed the village; provisions worth 52 rupees, gold armlets, and a mare were given.

At village Puniyad, Jivanji Maharaj held a feast for sadhus and saints in Vrindavan, and also held a feast at the Galta seat in Jaipur, and had a cow-shelter built for his own Barot; Samvat 1735, 125 rupees of banat (cloth) were given.

Shri Jivanji Maharaj departed for Satlok in Samvat 1737, Bhadarva Sud 5. Thirteen days later a feast was held; nine assemblies (mandals) from Vadodara were called, five akhadas of wrestlers came; 15,000 rupees were spent, five maunds of ghee, 250 rupees, and a gold cord were given. The Mahant of the seat was Shamdas Swamiji.

Mahant Vasantdas Swamiji held a feast at the footprint-shrine (charan-paduka) at village Sanja, Samvat 1886; 5,000 rupees were spent, and a shawl of 51 rupees was given.

At Puniyad, Bhagwandas Swamiji Maharaj held a feast; nine assemblies and five sweet dishes were prepared, Samvat 1875; 13,000 rupees were spent. Patel Govind Ramdas Tulsidas Mulji donated a cow-shed and fields. The name was recorded for the feast; gold bangles worth 125 rupees and an Ahmedabadi pitambar were given by Mahant Bhagwandas Swamiji.

Mahant Bhagwandas Swamiji had a bower (kunj) built at Vrindavan and also had a tulsi-bed made, and cooked a meal at Bansibat, Samvat 1858.

At Puniyad, the names of Gangabai, Kulbai, Jagannath Swamiji, Jamnabai, and Vakhatbai were recorded, Samvat 1923. Jagannath Swamiji held a feast, giving a gold bangle and a silk zari sari. Jagannath Swami went on pilgrimage to Dwarka and returned; he held a meal and a festival, Samvat 1922, on Kartak Vad 5.

Jagannath Swamiji had a bower built at Vrindavan and at Bansibat, and made a pilgrimage to Kashi, Samvat 1923; Jagannath Swami had the name of Gangabai recorded, 1938.

Kabirji Maharaj was born in Samvat 1414, and departed for Satlok in Samvat 1575."

_Magahar kiyo gavan, Magh shukla ekadashi mile pavan pavan_
(He went to Magahar; on the eleventh day of the bright half of the month of Magh, his breath merged into the cosmic breath — he passed away.)

Gnaniji's Guru lineage:

Ramanand, Anantanand, Gesji, Gnaniji, Gnandevji, Shamdevji, Ramdevji, Vasudevji, Narbheramji, Abheramji, Dayaramji, Rughnathdas Bhaibaba, Ramdas Hargovind Gopaldas, Gordhandas-Hansapura, Ramratandas, Sitaram, Ramkishandas Madhusudandas, Jugaldas, Jagdishdas.

"A tulsi-bed was built, Samvat 1889; Maharaj Jivandasji held a festival on Chaitra Sud 9; Sundardasji and Keshodasji of village Hansapura, Jivandasji patel of Origori (Kasampur), Vasandasji patel of village Bhoj, and [unclear] of village Puniyad and the patel of Tikam village, along with the whole assembly (panchamali), made grants — grazing land was donated and settled, and one maund of grain was donated, Samvat 1817. Maharaj Vitthaldas Swamiji, east and west; Kishanlal Swamiji alias Vasantdas.

Dwarkadas held feasts and fed the village, Samvat 1502, Chaitra Sud 8, Saturday. (Note: this Samvat is that of Dwarkadas, the Guru of Gnaniji.)"

"Bhagwandas Swami held feasts; Narsangdasji called nine assemblies, 1875; also Garibdas, Dharidas, Tulsidas."

The above is what is written in the genealogy ledger kept by the vahivancha (traditional genealogist-bard). The matter of Dada Sukhji calls for a great deal of further research. Haridas of Nadiad, in his Bhaktamal, Volume No. 44, page 31, writes in Kavit 1:

_Batak bijki mandmein, dekh bhaya man dhir_
_Dwarkadas updeshmein, sukhdata jetha bhaya ||4||_
(Meaning: Once, while urinating, Dwarkadasji, the Guru of Gnaniji, laughed on seeing a fig seed — the seed that gives rise to a tree as vast as a banyan — being swept away in the stream of urine. Seeing him laugh, Gnaniji also laughed; the Guru then asked why he had laughed. Gnaniji could give no answer, but later Kabirji explained: a tree as mighty as a banyan, which not even an elephant can uproot, has a seed that is carried helplessly away in urine — that is why the Guru had laughed. He who grasped this understanding, Gnaniji, became the disciple of the Guru Dwarkadas; and the great Dada Sukhji, also called Dada Jasvantji, became the one who received teaching from him and, in turn, bestowed it.)

The explanation of how "Sukhdata Jetha" comes to mean Dada Sukhji Jasvantji is found in the Kavit appearing in Handwritten Manuscript No. 37, page 137.

_Gyanike parmodhmein sukhdata Jasvantji bhaye_
_Take shikh Gopalji jan Jivankun updesh diyo ||5||_
(Meaning: The disciple who received Gnaniji's teaching was Sukhdata Jasvantji; his own disciple was Gopaldasji, who gave teaching to the devotee Jivanji.)

Thus, comparing the two, Sukhda Jasvantji comes to be Dada Jasvantji, also known as Dada Sukhji.

In "Nazar's Compilation" written by Nazar, Shamal Haribhai, Notebook No. 146, page 209, it is written:

"It appears that Jasvantji, the disciple of Gnaniji, must also have had the second name Dada Sakhaji (Sukhji). This seems so because in the earlier Kavit the name Jasvantji is found, and in the Guru lineage given in the Samagam, it is found as Dada Sakhji, of the Pipa lineage, resident of Shuklatirth. Considering everything, if each of these names belonged to a separate person, many years would have to have passed between them, and that does not seem possible; therefore it appears that all these names belong to one and the same person. This is also what Puniyad Swami Yadunathji holds, and on reflection it seems the same to me as well. Between Jivanji Maharaj and Gnaniji Maharaj, the one addressed as Gopaldas, Dada Sakhji, Dada Jasvant, and Sukhdata Jetha is one and the same person."

Gnaniji:

A whole essay could be written about Gnaniji, the Guru of Dada Sukhji, but let us look at it briefly. The true Guru Jivanji Maharaj has spoken about Gnaniji in Sakhi 129 of the Prabodh Ang:

_Gurjar khandma pragate, Gyani Gorakhnath_
_Das Kabire aayke, mastak dino hath ||6||_
(Meaning: Gorakhnath manifested in the region of Gujarat as Gnaniji; Das Kabir came and, placing his hand upon his head, bestowed grace and devotion upon him.)

_Gujaratmein Gyani bhaye, janat hai sab koy_
_Das Kabira aayke, darshan dina soy ||7||_
(Meaning: That a devotee such as Gnaniji appeared in Gujarat is a fact known to all; Das Kabirji came and blessed him with his darshan, making him fulfilled.)

In Handwritten Manuscript No. 31, page 205, the dialogue between Kabir and Gorakh is recorded; at its end, it is said that Gorakhnath, having lost, offered to Kabir the five symbols (matras) of Gorakhnath.

_Topi kopi kubadi jholi zhanda hath, kripa bhai Kabirki_
_Pancho matra sompi dinhi Gorakhnath ||8||_
(Meaning: The cap, the loincloth, the crutch-staff, the wallet, and the flag in hand — these the Gorakhpanthis keep. When Kabirji's grace descended, Gorakhnath handed over all five of these symbols to him.)

In a text composed under the title Garbhavali, Handwritten Register No. 208, from page 63, the discussion between Gorakh and Kabir is given. We have seen in the Kabir-Gorakh dialogue that Gorakh was defeated by Kabir. It is said that Gorakh, having attained 84 yogic powers (siddhis), came to conquer Kabir; sitting upon a trident, he began to say, "Debate with me." Then Kabirji held one end of a thread wound on a spinning spindle to the ground, flung the thread into the sky, and went and sat upon its far end, and told Gorakh, "Come and sit facing me." Then Gorakh, who had come to defeat him by the strength of his powers, admitted defeat and asked to be taught devotion (bhakti). Kabir then told Gorakh: "You have wasted your life on the path of yoga; but I will teach you devotion if you take another birth." It was for this reason that Gorakh came, taking birth as Gnaniji. In the text Garbhavali, the plea that Gorakh made to Kabir is described.

Gorakh Uvach (Gorakh said):

_Suno Swami garabh bandhana, kese hansa hoye chhutana_
_Kese mite jatharki trasa, so Saheb kaho ham pasa ||9||_
(Meaning: Gorakh said, "O Swami, listen — how does the swan-soul bound in the womb become free, and how does the torment of the womb-fire end? Tell me this, O Master.")

Sadguru Kabir Uvach (the true Guru Kabir said):

_Ab mein tumkun bhed batai, desh Murdharme janamo jai_
_Jesalmer Murdhar mojhara, Bhatike ghar lyo avatara_
_Gyani hoye jo naam tumhara, Khoji guruko lev bichara_
_Phir aavo Gujarat mojhara, Kanam mandal sidh bhom bandhana_
_Jaanha hoye tumaro asthana, in dehise tohe samujhai_
_Tumharo panth bichal sab jai, tumaro bhekh chale sansara_
_Mein tumhare jivka karo ubara, tum to bund sadhna kinha_
_Bhag dekhi tum bohot darana, tate garabhavasme aai_
_Tumharo panth gaman hi pai, Gorakh manme esi aai_
_Deh dharu Sindhmo jai, Chhatri ghar leu avatara_
_Jugat jugatse karu ubara_

[Sakhi]
_Kahe Gorakh Sadguru suno, mein leu avatar_
_Phir tum hamkun kaise milo, so guru kaho bichar_
_Kar jodi Gorakh kahe, sunho Swami sujan_
_Sharan tumhari mohi rakh ho, dyo apna nij gyan_

[Kabir vachan]
_Kabir kahe Khoji mutat hans uthe, tum hi haso apar_
_Tab Khoji man sanse pare, tumse bujh bichar_
_Jab tum hamkun khoj ho, ham tumkun dehi didar_
_Khojika sansa mite, sehje hoye ubar_
_Batak bijki mandme, dekh bhayo man dhir_
_Jan Gyanika sanse mita, Sadguru mile Kabir_
_Kahe Kabir suno Gorakha, mano vachan hamar_
_Nij gyan samjhavahu, dusar janam tumhar_
_So Jesalmer janamiya, Bhathi kul Rajput_
_Gurjar dhar (desh) pavan kiyo, so Gyani gun avdhut_

(Meaning: The true Guru Kabir said: Now I tell you the secret — go and take birth in the land of Murdhar. There, in Jaisalmer within Murdhar, take incarnation in a Bhati household. Your name will be Gyani (Gnaniji), and you shall take the teaching of the Guru Khojiji. Afterward, come into Gujarat, and dwell in the fine, level land of the Kanam region, wherever your abode is to be. And I myself, in this very body of Kabir, will instruct you, and your entire Gorakh-panth will be shaken and drawn away toward devotion; and the path (bhekh) of devotion that you take up there will spread through the world. I will bring about the deliverance of your soul — but right now you are practising the discipline of celibacy, preserving the seed, and, seeing the womb, you are greatly afraid, and so you will come into the womb. Thinking of going by your path, that is, Kabirji's path, this thought arose in Gorakh's mind: "Let me take a body and be born in Sindh, taking incarnation in a Kshatriya household, and by various means bring about my own deliverance."

Sakhi: Gorakh began to say: "True Guru, listen — I shall indeed take birth, but afterward, how will I meet you? Explain this to me, Guru."

With joined hands Gorakh said: "O all-knowing Swami, listen — keep me in your refuge, and give me the teaching of your own knowledge."

Kabirji's word — Kabir said: "When Khojiji laughs while urinating, you too will burst out laughing without restraint. Then Khojiji will be puzzled: 'I laughed, but why did you laugh? Tell me the reason for my laughter.' And so, when you set out to seek me in order to find that reason, I will grant you my darshan, and the doubt that Khojiji had raised for you will be resolved, and your deliverance will come about easily."

Seeing the seed of a banyan's fig swept away in urine, Khojiji's mind was struck with wonder; and when the true Guru Kabir was met, the resolution came to the doubt about the question Gnaniji had asked — that as long as the seed remained attached to the tree it was safe, but once separated from the tree it is swept away in filth and urine. In the same way, the soul (jiva) remains safe as long as it is attached to the feet of the Lord; but turning away from God, it drifts about in the ocean of worldly existence, in the filth of the womb. The tree is contained within the seed, and the seed is contained within the tree; in the same way, the world is interwoven with God, and God with the world.

Kabir then said: "Gorakh, heed what I say — I will explain my own true knowledge to you in your next incarnation."

Thus this Gorakh was born in Jaisalmer, in a Bhatia Rajput family, and this Gnaniji, possessed of the qualities of an avadhut, sanctified the region of Gujarat.)

The devotional hymn (pad) written about Gorakhnath by Dayaldas, the Udabhagat of Vayadapol, introduces us to Gnaniji. Nazar has translated the verses of that hymn relating to Gnaniji, as follows:

"Gorakhji sought teaching from Kabir; Gorakhji shed his old garb. Gorakh was born in the land of Murdhar, where he was named Chatursangh. At the age of 11, Chatur Sangh was to be given the royal coronation-mark (rajtilak), but Chatur Sangh thought, 'I have taken this body for devotion; if I take up rule I shall fall into the snare of maya, and shall have to face a dark end.' So, at midnight, he left that place and, coming into Gujarat, at the pond-bank of village Sokhda, took up the garb of an ascetic and rested there. Each day a Brahmin woman used to bring him food; that woman's son died, and Chatursangh brought the son back to life. After this, Chatursangh left Sokhda (the name of the next village is worn away and cannot be read) .... and went and met Dwarkadasji. He showed Chatursangh the Name of Ram. Once, Dwarkadas laughed, and so Chatursangh laughed too. Chatursangh set out to discover the reason for the laughter. Meditating on the island (bet) of the Reva [Narmada], he performed austerities for seven days; one morning, at sunrise, Kabirji, after cleaning his teeth with a twig, planted the split twig, and it grew into a banyan tree. Chatursangh left off his meditation and bowed at his feet; Kabirji then revealed the secret to him, and Chatursangh went to Dwarkadas and said:"

_Dayala vari utarat behe gayo, vatko bij chanik_
_Tab gurudev yun boliya, baat kahi te nik ||10||_
(Meaning: Dayaldas writes: "While urinating, the seed of the little banyan fig was swept away — that is why you laughed." Then the Guru said, "Now you have spoken the truth correctly.")

"After this, both Chatursangh and Dwarkadasji came to Kabirji, and Kabirji explained to both of them the teaching of the Agam-panth."

This is how Nazar has translated this hymn. Revered Yadunath Maharaj, in the Shubh Sangraha file, has recorded the following note about Gnaniji:

Ramkabir, 2-12-29:

Chi. Chatursinh (Gnaniji), son of Motisinh, king of Jaisalmer (Marwad), when the time came for his marriage, refused his father, saying, "I have not come to rule a kingdom, but to worship God and lead others to worship Him." When many kings sent marriage proposals and each was refused, people began to wonder: since he is refusing the daughters of all these kings, what can be on his mind — is he perhaps going to marry a girl from outside the caste? To settle this, all the kings gathered together at Udaipur in Mewad. At that time the Rana of Udaipur was Jasvantsinh; he sent a proposal to Jaisalmer for his own daughter, Gangabai. The king of Jaisalmer persuaded the prince that a proposal from such a good family could not be turned down. Chatursinh refused, but when his father would not agree, he asked that the wedding turmeric (pithi) be applied only to the thumb of his right hand. The wedding party (jaan) went to Udaipur for the marriage, but as soon as the fourth round of the wedding circumambulation was completed, Gnaniji fled and came to Jaipur.

The account of Jaipur:

The king of Jaipur had earlier been a disciple of a Kanphata ascetic (Kanphatas are of two kinds — those who keep rings in the ear; one kind keeps rings of glass in the ear. In this tradition, when the ear is completely split by a heavy ring, one is to take living samadhi — living samadhi is given). That king had a rule that he would not eat food without first having darshan of his Guru Maharaj or of his ring. The Maharaj's ashram was far outside the city, but at night he would not let any traveller stay there. Yet, if anyone did stay, at night he would take the form of a tiger and kill them. It happened that some old Vaishnav mahatma came there; but this Kanphata mahant told the saint to go back into the city at night. But the saint said, "I will stay here tonight and go in the morning." At night, the king's Kanphata Guru took the form of a tiger and came to kill the mahatma. But because of the radiance of the Vaishnav saint, he could not come near. When he began to make trouble from a distance, the saint sprinkled a handful of water and turned him into the form of a donkey; he also made the ring in his ear, and the ring kept in a box, disappear. In the morning, when the king came for darshan, though he searched for his Guru, the Maharaj could not be found, nor could the ring be found. He then asked the old mahatma, who told him, "Look in the ravines — something may be grazing there." The king saw his own Guru grazing in the form of a donkey and prostrated himself before the saint. He then brought the saint to his palace and asked to take discipleship. The saint agreed on the following conditions: that a temple of Ramji be built on this spot, that his people bring five bundles of firewood every day, and that the king become his disciple. This practice continues to this day. That mahatma had two disciples. Gnaniji Maharaj, having fled from the wedding pavilion, came to the chief disciple of that mahatma, Geshji (Khojiji) Maharaj, and asked to be given initiation (diksha). The Maharaj said, "Here, initiation is given to fakirs, not to the wealthy." Gnaniji took off his own ornaments and took initiation. Then he asked for service to perform; he was given oversight of the temple servants. Afterward he asked for another service, and was given the task of fanning Thakorji. At that time, a ship belonging to one of the Maharaj's disciples was sinking, and Gnaniji, perceiving the inclination of his Guru's mind, showed him the trick of, after placing the crown on the image, also placing the garland the right way. Because of this, the Guru named him Gnaniji. He was then given leave to go and see the world, and was given seven things: 1. the invisible cap — the quilt of knowledge (Gyan-godadi); 2. the boon of fearlessness (abhay-vadan); 3. the knowledge of reviving the dead (mrut sanjivani vidya); 4. the knowledge of restoring severed limbs (angabhang vidya); 5. the power to make one's word come true (vachan siddhi); 6. the Varun mantra; and seventh, that he should then go to Shuklatirth. There he was to meet Nirvan Sahib and Kabirji. Kabir Sahib was to show him that there was no solitary place for him to stay; so, by the Varun mantra, land was to be sought near the Narmada, and Dharmadas was to grant him the island. Nirvanji warned him about Surat. There, harassment by Muslims was to occur, and Gnaniji was to be saved; Gnaniji was to go to Manipur. He was to live between the slaughterhouse quarter and the courtesans' quarter, where he would be persecuted. Seven hundred and fifty were to be brought back to life, and the sugar of the caravan-trader (vanjara) was to be turned to salt. The Muslim soldiers were to seek him out, and among them the Sultan's soldier was to die. On this there is still to this day a dreadful shrine (dargah) built by hand. In Register No. 283, in the book on the pilgrimage of Hindustan, on page 55, it is written: "Here the king is a Yaduvanshi Rajput. King Rao Jesal founded this city in the year 1156 CE. The king has the honor of a 15-gun salute."

Natvarlal, the 15th successor of Gnaniji's lineage at Mota Sanja, writes on page 100 of a long letter that he wrote: "I am writing this from what is written in the hand of Bapuji Ramkishandasji.

Note taken from the vahivancha's ledger:

Birthplace: Prayagraj (Ramanandji), a Kanyakubja Brahmin, the founding figure (mool purush) of the Galta seat of Jaipur, a Jagadguru, born Samvat 1356, Magh Vad 6, Sunday. Disciple of Ramanandji was Anantanandji; disciple of Anantanandji was Gesji, also called Khojiji; and the disciple of Khojiji was Shri Maharaj Gnaniji, also called Gnanacharya, through the seat at Mota Sanja. (This birth date may be that of Khojiji; he may have been a Brahmin.)

Vahivancha Keshavray, in an inland letter dated 4-1-58 written to Ramkishandas, the Mahant of Mota Sanja, has recorded the genealogy of Gnaniji; in it he writes:

'The institution (sansthan), village Sanja, taluka Jhagadia, district Bharuch, via Ankleshwar, post Sanja. The founding figure, Shri Gnaniji Maharaj, first arrived there in Samvat 1968.'"

Natvarlal writes on page 99 of his long letter:

Having set out from Jaisalmer, Gehji Maharaj set out together with Gnaniji Maharaj. The king of that region followed the Jain faith. They were staying overnight in the forest of some kingdom. That king had gone out hunting, and as evening approached he lost his way. Gnaniji and Gehji Maharaj were in the forest at that time; the king came to Gnaniji and Gehji Maharaj and said, "I wish to stay here for the night — if you will let me, I shall stay." Gnaniji said, "If you wish to stay, then stay." So the king tied up his horse and got down. Gnaniji then told the king, "Come, please eat." But the king said, "I follow the Jain faith, and since the day is about to end, I shall not eat." Then Gnaniji lifted up the served plate and held it back, so that it seemed to the king that there were still two ghadis [about 48 minutes] of daylight left. The king said, "There are still two ghadis of daylight, so let me eat." The king then sat down to eat, and by the time he finished eating and rose, he realized that two ghadis of the night had already passed. The king then thought, "This must be some miraculous person." So the king said to Gnaniji, "Please stay here, and take whatever you need from us — only please stay here." But Gnaniji said, "It is good for a sadhu to keep moving on." So Gnaniji Maharaj set off from there and came to Jaipur. Since the king of Jaipur's Guru was a Kanphata, Gnaniji lay down in the outskirts of Jaipur, having lit a dhuni (sacred fire). The Kanphata then thought to himself, "This must be some miraculous person, and if any miracle of Gnaniji Maharaj becomes known, the king will remove me from the position of Guru." So the Kanphata sent someone to tell Gnaniji, "It would be better if you went elsewhere from here." Then Gnaniji Maharaj and Geshji Maharaj tied up the burning dhuni in a cloth, took it, and went far away, and set the burning dhuni down there and stayed. But the Kanphata thought to himself, "It would be good if I killed this holy man." So at night he sent, by means of a mantra, a stone weighing twelve maunds. Gnaniji realized that this stone had been sent to kill him, so Gnaniji raised his tongs (chipiyo), and the stone broke into pieces. Gnaniji then thought that he too should show some miracle. So, by mantra, Gnaniji brought under his own bedding the rings of all the Kanphatas, from the senior-most down to the junior-most; but he left in place the ring of the senior Kanphata, the king's own Guru, and instead turned him into a donkey. In the morning, when the king went for the darshan of his Guru, he could not find him. So he asked someone, and was told that some holy man had come to the edge of the village, and that his Guru might have gone to him. So the king, searching for Gnaniji, came to him and asked. Gnaniji Maharaj said, "Brother, your Guru must have turned into a donkey." The king then saw a donkey grazing, and recognized it by the ring in its ear. He then thought: "If my Guru cannot even save himself, how can he save me or grant me liberation?" And he said, "I do not want such a Guru — my Guru is Gnaniji." This much I know, and this much I write. — Written by J. U. Natvarlal, page 102 of his letter.

Excerpt from the newspaper "Pratap," dated 11-7-1974, Ashadh Vad 6, Thursday.

"Let us solve the historical puzzle of 'Bava Ghor' (While on personal work in Rajpipla, the enthusiastic researcher of the college there, Dr. Kantikumar Bhatt (M.A., Ph.D., Sahityaratna), spoke about the details he had gathered on 'Bava Ghor.' These have been presented here for reading. Researchers throughout Gujarat are especially invited to present a verified history on this subject. — Editor.

In Bharuch district, near Jhagadia, there is a village named Ratanpur. Up until the fourteenth century of the Vikram era, it was a large, prosperous town. Nearby there is a hill known as the 'Bava Ghor' hill. On that hill is the tomb (majar) of 'Bava Ghor.' Investigating who Bava Ghor was, various different accounts are found. These accounts differ so much from one another that no single common fact can be established from them.

Shri Ramanlal Shah of Ranipara village, near Jhagadia, in his account of Gnaniji, has identified Bava Ghor as Gnaniji's bodyguard. This Gnaniji was originally a prince of Jaisalmer. Moved by a spirit of renunciation, he fled from the wedding altar and came to the site of Kabirvad. There he took initiation from Kabir Sahib. His seat is at Mota Sanja, very close to Bava Ghor. The king of Jaisalmer had sent the bodyguard Bava Sahib to search for him. When he came here, he was practising yoga in the thicket of Shulpaneshwar. Despite his father's efforts, he did not return. Baba Sahib stayed here along with Gnaniji's betrothed wife, Gangakuvarba. It is said that the land that was given to this Baba Sahib in Jaisalmer still runs in the name of his descendants to this day. No other evidence is found to confirm this account.

The second account is entirely different from this one........"

Natvarlal's letter, on page 111, records:

Dictated by Prahladdasji, disciple of Kundandasji:

Four accomplished ones (siddha purush) came from Uttarkhand — Gnaniji Maharaj, Kabirji, Nirvan, and Tejanand. Kabirji remained on the island (bet) of Kabirvad in the Narmada. Before going to Mota Sanja, Gnaniji Maharaj stayed for a while where there was then forest. Tejanand went to Kharvasa, and Nirvan Sahib made his abode in Surat.

Gnaniji Maharaj began his devotional practice (bhajan) and, in order to bathe, built a well; water rose up from the ground of its own accord, over the parapet, and flowed out. Gnaniji Maharaj used to bathe every day from this well that he had built; the well still stands there.

(Note: This is written on page 37 of the letter.)

_Pani chhe amap patalka, nicha daman kup_
_Bhajanke pratapse, Varundev aaya up ||11||_
(Meaning: There is immeasurable water in the netherworld, lying deep below the well; but by the power of devotional practice, that water — Varun Dev, the deity of water — rose up to the top of the well.)

After cleaning his teeth with a neem twig, he planted it split into two; it is said to still be alive — that neem is sweet in taste, and the split into two branches can still be seen. By his power, a fair (melo) is held for a month; there, Udabhagats and sadhu-saints gather with great devotion. The fair is held from Posh Sud 11. Groups of devotees come to the fair from far away — from Surat, Charotar, Vadodara, and Bharuch districts — and there is great rejoicing and celebration. After Gnaniji Maharaj took samadhi, Rai Gnandevji Maharaj remained as successor. His wife also came here; though he had renounced married life after their marriage, being devoted to her husband (pativrata), she came here, and only when she met Rai Gnandev did she take food and water. Bava Ghor became a disciple.....

In a manuscript obtained from Gnaniji's seat at Mota Sanja, No. 5, page 276, it is written that in Samvat 1444, Shri Gnaniji Maharaj took samadhi here, during the reign of Rajjit Sigji of Nandod. (Note: There is an error in the Samvat date.)

In the third volume of the four large volumes of the Bhaktamal published by Ramanand Pustakalaya, Sudamapuri, Vrindavan, it is shown as though Khojiji himself were Gnaniji. But this institution evidently did not have information about Mota Sanja, and so, in the couplet about the "batak bij ki mand" (banyan-seed), instead of writing "Jan Gnanika sansa mita" (the devotee Gnani's doubt was resolved), they wrote "Khojika sanshay mita" (Khoji's doubt was resolved), and explained the Batak-bij couplet in this way, as follows:

_Batak bijmein vad base, mool daal phal phool_
_Gyani guru parsad te, pakda jab nij mool ||12||_
(from the Gyani Granthavali)
(Meaning: Within the seed of the banyan dwell the banyan tree, its roots, branches, fruit, and flower. Having understood all this by the grace of the Guru, I have taken refuge in the original Supreme Brahman who fashions both the tree and the seed.)

The doubt indeed belonged to both Gnaniji and his Guru Khojiji, but the author of this couplet is Gnaniji himself.

As for the earlier episode concerning the Kanphata written about in connection with Gnaniji, that same episode is shown, in the second volume of the Vrindavan Bhaktamal, in the life-account of Krishnadas Payahari — a Guru in Gnaniji's own Guru lineage — as one where it was Krishnadas who subdued the Kanphata. Thus, many kinds of differing variations are found in the Bhaktamal, but these episodes do belong to these great souls.

In the Bhaktamal, the names of 35 Gurus in total, in the Guru lineage of Jivanji Maharaj, are given. Among them, the life-accounts of 9 Gurus are not found in Nabha Swami's Bhaktamal; but since the Gurus of the lineage after Dwarkadasji belong to five generations later than Nabha Swami, we have already seen, among the information we have about the Gurus from Gnaniji down to Jivanji Maharaj, the accounts of Gnaniji and Dada Sukhji. Thus, of the nine generations of Gurus after Dwarkadas, no mention is found in the Bhaktamal; but let us look at a brief account of those about whom the Bhaktamal does have something written.

Narharidasji:

Once he went for the darshan of Jagannathji. There he thought that if he performed a full prostration (sashtang dandavat) before Thakorji, that much time of darshan would be lost; so instead he bowed with his feet toward the deity. Seeing this as improper conduct, the temple priests (pandas) seized him by the feet and dragged him out of the temple. But by Jagannathji's gracious command, everyone then honored him.

Sariramdasji:

Once, near Chitrakoot, in a village named Tvarra, [he went] to warn the people there...
